scope: 20 existing short first-school-mock AQA Chemistry AS and taught A2 recall cards across rate orders, entropy, Period 3 ionisation, equilibrium, calorimetry, esters, carboxylic acids, back titrations and RP3
purpose: Precise accepted paraphrase and explicit wrong answer calibration of untouched original IDs. No new cards, deferred Chemistry buffers or multi-mark flashcards.
safety: Apply exact id, Chemistry subject, original AS/A2 stage, mock=true, unchanged front and back, active guard.
Retain all pre-existing accept/reject entries and saved-progress keys.
Check every model answer, acceptable paraphrase and specific misconception against production evaluator.
Do not infer whole AQA mock completion from a sample of 20 cards.
Review free-form explanations and physical diagrams independently.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What is the rate-determining step?
rows.originalBack: The slow elementary step that limits overall reaction rate.
accept: The slowest elementary stage in a multi-step mechanism, controlling the overall reaction rate.
reject: The fastest elementary reaction step determines the overall rate.
The final reaction step must always be rate determining regardless of its speed.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What is standard entropy?
rows.originalBack: Absolute entropy of 1 mol of substance at stated standard conditions.
accept: The absolute entropy per mole of a substance in its standard state under standard conditions.
reject: The enthalpy change when one mole of the substance burns completely.
The entropy change on cooling one mole of substance to absolute zero.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What does positive ΔS mean?
rows.originalBack: The system's entropy increases.
accept: The entropy of the system has increased, so its change in entropy is positive.
reject: A positive entropy change means the entropy of the system falls.
Positive delta S guarantees the reaction is feasible at any temperature.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What is a zero-order reaction with respect to A?
rows.originalBack: Rate is independent of [A].
accept: At fixed other conditions, changing the concentration of A has no effect on reaction rate.
reject: A zero-order reaction has rate directly proportional to A concentration.
Zero order means the reaction mixture contains no A molecules.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What is a first-order reaction with respect to A?
rows.originalBack: Rate is proportional to [A].
accept: At fixed other conditions doubling A concentration doubles the rate.
reject: Doubling A concentration causes a fourfold increase in rate for first order.
First order in A means rate has no dependence on A concentration.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What is a second-order reaction with respect to A?
rows.originalBack: Rate is proportional to [A]².
accept: At constant other conditions doubling the concentration of A increases rate by a factor of four.
reject: Second order in A means doubling its concentration only doubles rate.
For second order in A the rate decreases when its concentration increases.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Why is the first ionisation energy of Al below Mg?
rows.originalBack: Al loses a higher-energy 3p electron.
accept: The electron removed from aluminium is in a higher-energy 3p subshell than the magnesium 3s electron.
reject: Aluminium has a lower first ionisation energy because it loses a 2p electron.
The first electron removed from aluminium is in 3s while magnesium loses 3p.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Why is the first ionisation energy of S below P?
rows.originalBack: Paired 3p electrons repel, easing removal.
accept: Sulfur has a pair of electrons in a 3p orbital that repel one another, making removal easier than in phosphorus.
reject: Sulfur has a lower first ionisation energy because it removes an electron from a 4s orbital.
Phosphorus has more 3p electron pairing repulsion than sulfur, causing sulfur to lose an electron more easily.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What defines dynamic equilibrium?
rows.originalBack: Forward and reverse reaction rates are equal in a closed system.
accept: In a closed system, the forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates.
reject: At dynamic equilibrium, both reactions stop completely.
At dynamic equilibrium the reactant and product concentrations must be equal.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: How does a catalyst affect the equilibrium position?
rows.originalBack: It does not change it.
accept: A catalyst changes the rate of attaining equilibrium but not its position.
reject: A catalyst pushes the equilibrium to the product side permanently.
Catalysts raise Kc and favour products at a fixed temperature.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: How does increased pressure shift gaseous equilibrium?
rows.originalBack: Towards the side with fewer gas molecules.
accept: Raising gas pressure favours the equilibrium side with fewer moles of gas.
reject: Raising pressure always shifts gas equilibrium to the side with more gas molecules.
Pressure increases equilibrium constant Kc while temperature is held constant.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Why might calorimetry give a smaller temperature rise than expected?
rows.originalBack: Some energy is transferred to the surroundings.
accept: Some of the reaction heat is lost to the surroundings, reducing the measured temperature change.
reject: The calorimeter always gains extra heat from the surroundings so the measured rise must be larger.
A lower measured rise proves that no energy is exchanged with the surroundings.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Why is extrapolation used in some temperature–time graphs?
rows.originalBack: To estimate temperature change before heat exchange distorts it.
accept: Extend the cooling trend back to the mixing time to estimate the corrected temperature change.
reject: Extrapolation is used to replace every measured reading by the same final temperature.
Extrapolation makes the heat loss exactly zero during the entire experiment.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What is the general equation for esterification?
rows.originalBack: Carboxylic acid + alcohol ⇌ ester + water.
accept: Alcohol and carboxylic acid react reversibly to produce an ester and water.
reject: An aldehyde and a ketone react to produce an ester and water.
A carboxylic acid and alcohol react to give an alkane and carbon dioxide.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What are fats and vegetable oils made from chemically?
rows.originalBack: Triglycerides containing three ester links to glycerol.
accept: They are triglycerides, with glycerol joined to three fatty acids by ester bonds.
reject: Fats and oils are peptide chains joined by amide bonds.
Vegetable oils consist exclusively of unbonded free glycerol and free fatty acids.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What structural feature makes a fatty acid unsaturated?
rows.originalBack: At least one carbon–carbon double bond in the chain.
accept: A fatty acid is unsaturated if the hydrocarbon chain has at least one C=C bond.
reject: Unsaturated fatty acids contain only carbon carbon single bonds in their chains.
A fatty acid is unsaturated solely because it contains the carbonyl bond of COOH.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What is the carboxyl functional group?
rows.originalBack: –COOH.
accept: The carboxyl group is C(=O)OH, usually written as COOH.
reject: A carboxylic acid has the ester functional group COOR instead of COOH.
The carboxyl group is a carbon carbon double bond C=C.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What causes the acidity of a carboxylic acid?
rows.originalBack: It can donate a proton from –COOH.
accept: The COOH group can release H+ to form a carboxylate ion.
reject: Carboxylic acids are acidic because they always gain a proton from water.
The hydrocarbon chain donates a proton while the COOH group never does.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Why must dilution factors be applied in a back titration?
rows.originalBack: An aliquot represents only a fraction of the total diluted solution.
accept: The measured aliquot is only part of the diluted solution, so scale up its moles by the total-volume to aliquot-volume ratio.
reject: The amount of reagent in the aliquot is always the same as in the whole diluted mixture.
When the total volume is larger than the aliquot, divide the aliquot moles by total volume over aliquot volume.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Why must the same visual endpoint be used for rate comparisons?
rows.originalBack: So results represent a consistent extent of reaction.
accept: Use the same visible endpoint so the times represent the same extent of reaction.
reject: Using the same endpoint makes all reactions finish completely regardless of conditions.
Using an identical endpoint eliminates all random timing errors.
